stem: The table shows the preferred lunch of 200 students, by grade level. How many of the students are in Grade 10 and prefer a packed lunch?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This is the number of students in Grade 9 who prefer a packed lunch.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is the row total, the number of students in Grade 10 who prefer either type of lunch.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is the column total, the number of students in either grade who prefer a packed lunch.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The cell in the row for Grade 10 and the column for packed lunch is 90.

explanation: Read the cell where the row for Grade 10 meets the column for packed lunch: 90 students.

diagram.caption: Preferred lunch of 200 students, by grade level

stem: Which of the following displays can be used to show the relationship between two categorical variables?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A boxplot, with a box showing the middle 50% of the values of the first variable for each of the categories
choices.explanation: A boxplot summarizes a quantitative variable using its five-number summary.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A dotplot, with one dot for each of the individuals above the values of the first variable on a number line
choices.explanation: A dotplot shows the values of one quantitative variable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A histogram, with each bar showing the frequency of the values of the first variable that fall in an interval of the number line
choices.explanation: A histogram displays the distribution of a single quantitative variable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A segmented bar chart, with one bar for each level of the first variable divided into segments for the levels of the second variable
choices.explanation: A segmented bar chart shows the distribution of one categorical variable within each level of the other.

explanation: Side-by-side bar charts, segmented bar charts and mosaic plots display two categorical variables.

stem: The side-by-side bar chart shows, for the students in each grade level, the proportion who prefer a cafeteria lunch and the proportion who prefer a packed lunch. Which of the following statements is supported by the graph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: There are more students in Grade 10 than in Grade 9, because the Grade 10 bar for packed lunch is taller
choices.explanation: The graph shows relative frequencies within each grade, so it does not show the number of students in a grade.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A greater proportion of the students in Grade 9 than of the students in Grade 10 prefer a packed lunch
choices.explanation: The Grade 9 bar for packed lunch (0.40) is shorter than the Grade 10 bar (0.75).

choices.label: C
choices.text: A greater proportion of the students in Grade 10 than of the students in Grade 9 prefer a packed lunch
choices.explanation: The bar for packed lunch is 0.75 for Grade 10 and 0.40 for Grade 9.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The same proportion of the students in each grade prefer a packed lunch, because the bars for each grade add to 1
choices.explanation: The bars add to 1 within each grade, but the packed lunch bars are not the same height.

explanation: The graph compares the distribution of lunch preference across the levels of grade: 0.75 compared with 0.40 prefer a packed lunch.

diagram.altText: Side-by-side bar chart of the relative frequencies of the preferred lunch, for each grade level: Grade 9 cafeteria 0.60, packed 0.40; Grade 10 cafeteria 0.25, packed 0.75.

stem: In a segmented bar chart, there is one bar for each grade level, and each bar is divided into segments for the preferred lunch. The segments are in about the same proportions in every bar. Which of the following is the best conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The bars have the same number of students in each of the grade levels in the chart
choices.explanation: The proportions can be the same even when the bars are for groups of different sizes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The grade level causes the students to have the preferred lunch that they have
choices.explanation: A graph of two categorical variables cannot show that one variable causes the other.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There is strong evidence of an association between the grade level and the preferred lunch
choices.explanation: An association would show as segments with different proportions from one bar to another.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There is little or no evidence of an association between the grade level and the preferred lunch
choices.explanation: If the distribution of one variable is about the same at every level of the other variable, the variables do not appear to be associated.

explanation: The variables are associated when the distribution of one changes across the levels of the other; here it does not change.

stem: A student looks at the table and says, "More students in Grade 10 prefer a packed lunch than in Grade 9, since 90 is greater than 32, so Grade 10 students are more likely to prefer a packed lunch." Which of the following is the best response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The student cannot compare the grades, because a two-way table cannot be used to compare two groups of students
choices.explanation: A two-way table is used to compare the distributions of one variable across the levels of another.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The groups are different sizes, so the student should compare the proportions: 90 / 120 = 0.75 for Grade 10 and 32 / 80 = 0.40 for Grade 9
choices.explanation: Counts from groups of different sizes should be compared using relative frequencies. Here the conclusion is correct but the reason is not.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The student is incorrect, because the proportions are 0.75 for Grade 9 and 0.40 for Grade 10 in this table
choices.explanation: The proportion who prefer a packed lunch is 0.75 for Grade 10 and 0.40 for Grade 9.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The student is correct, because a greater count always shows a greater proportion in two groups of any sizes that the student compares
choices.explanation: A greater count does not show a greater proportion when the groups have different sizes.

explanation: To justify a claim about two groups of different sizes, compare relative frequencies: 0.75 and 0.40.

diagram.caption: Preferred lunch of 200 students, by grade level

stem: What do the entries in the cells of a two-way table show?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The correlation between the two variables for the individuals that have each of the levels of the first variable
choices.explanation: A correlation is for two quantitative variables.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The five-number summary of the values of one of the variables for each of the levels of the other variable
choices.explanation: A five-number summary is for a quantitative variable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The mean of a quantitative variable for the individuals in each of the groups that are formed by the two categorical variables in the table
choices.explanation: Cells of a two-way table are counts or proportions, not means of a quantitative variable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The frequency (count) or the relative frequency of the individuals that have a particular level of each of the two categorical variables
choices.explanation: Each cell is for one combination of a level of one variable and a level of the other.

explanation: The entries in the cells are frequencies or relative frequencies.

stem: A researcher records, for 300 adults, whether each lives in a city or in the country, and whether each prefers to read books on paper or on a screen. The numbers of adults in the two living groups are not equal. Which of the following displays is best for comparing the reading preference of the two living groups?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A boxplot of the reading preferences, with one box for each of the living groups that the researcher studied
choices.explanation: A boxplot is for a quantitative variable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A segmented bar chart of counts, because the heights of the segments for the two groups can be compared directly
choices.explanation: When the groups have different sizes, counts are hard to compare.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A histogram of the number of adults in each of the living groups, with the bars placed next to each other
choices.explanation: A histogram is for a quantitative variable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A segmented bar chart of relative frequencies, with one bar for each living group and the segments showing the proportions that prefer paper and screen
choices.explanation: Relative frequencies adjust for groups of different sizes, so the segments can be compared directly.

explanation: To compare the distribution of one variable across groups of different sizes, use relative frequencies.

stem: The table shows the main way of getting news of 400 adults, by age group. What is the joint relative frequency of adults who are under 40 and get their news mainly online?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A joint relative frequency is a cell divided by the table total: 120 / 400 = 0.30.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is the conditional relative frequency among the adults under 40: 120 / 200.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is the marginal relative frequency of getting news online: 180 / 400.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is the conditional relative frequency among the adults who get news online: 120 / 180.

explanation: Joint relative frequency = 120 / 400 = 0.30.

diagram.caption: Main way of getting news, for 400 adults

stem: The table shows the main way of getting news of 400 adults, by age group. What is the marginal relative frequency of adults who get their news mainly online?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This is the proportion of the adults under 40 who get news online, a conditional relative frequency.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is 180 / 200, which divides the column total by the size of only one of the age groups.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is the joint relative frequency of adults who are under 40 and get news online: 120 / 400.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A marginal relative frequency is a column total divided by the table total: 180 / 400 = 0.45.

explanation: Marginal relative frequency = 180 / 400 = 0.45.

diagram.caption: Main way of getting news, for 400 adults

stem: The table shows the main way of getting news of 400 adults, by age group. Among the adults who are under 40, what proportion get their news mainly online?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This restricts to the adults who get news online instead of to the adults under 40: 120 / 180.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Restrict to the row for adults under 40 and divide the cell by the row total: 120 / 200 = 0.60.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is the proportion of all of the adults who get news online, which ignores age.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This divides by the table total (400), which is the joint relative frequency.

explanation: Conditional relative frequency = 120 / 200 = 0.60.

diagram.caption: Main way of getting news, for 400 adults

stem: The table shows the main way of getting news of 400 adults, by age group. Among the adults who get their news mainly online, what proportion are under 40?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This restricts to the adults under 40 instead of to the adults who get news online: 120 / 200.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This divides by the table total (400), which is the joint relative frequency.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is the proportion of the adults who get news online who are 40 or over: 60 / 180.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Restrict to the column for online and divide the cell by the column total: 120 / 180 = 0.67.

explanation: Conditional relative frequency = 120 / 180, which is about 0.67.

diagram.caption: Main way of getting news, for 400 adults

stem: The table shows the main way of getting news of 400 adults, by age group. Which of the following is a correct comparison of the two age groups?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The two age groups have the same distribution of the main way of getting news, because each age group has 200 adults
choices.explanation: The group sizes are equal, but the distributions of the main way are different.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The adults under 40 are more likely to get their news mainly from print, because 30% of them do, compared with 15% of the adults who are 40 or over
choices.explanation: This is reversed. Print is 30 of 200 (15%) for the adults under 40 and 60 of 200 (30%) for the adults who are 40 or over.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The adults who are 40 or over are more likely to get their news mainly online, because 80 is the greatest count in their row
choices.explanation: The 80 is the count for television. Online is 60 of the 200 adults who are 40 or over, which is 30%.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The adults under 40 are more likely to get their news mainly online, because 60% of them do, compared with 30% of the adults who are 40 or over
choices.explanation: The conditional relative frequencies, 120 / 200 and 60 / 200, show that the distributions differ, which is evidence of an association.

explanation: Compare the conditional distributions: online 0.60 and 0.30, television 0.25 and 0.40, print 0.15 and 0.30.

diagram.caption: Main way of getting news, for 400 adults

stem: The table shows the results of an exam in two classes. Which of the following is the best conclusion about the relationship between the class and passing the exam?

choices.label: A
choices.text: There is evidence of an association, because more students in Class 2 passed the exam than in Class 1
choices.explanation: The counts are different because the classes have different sizes. The proportions that passed are equal.

choices.label: B
choices.text: There is evidence of an association, because the number who did not pass is different in the two classes
choices.explanation: The counts differ only because the classes have different sizes. The proportions that did not pass are both 0.40.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The evidence of an association cannot be found, because a two-way table has no relative frequencies in it
choices.explanation: Relative frequencies can be calculated from the counts of a two-way table.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There is no evidence of an association, because the proportion who passed is 0.60 in each class
choices.explanation: The conditional relative frequencies are 60 / 100 = 0.60 and 90 / 150 = 0.60, the same for both classes.

explanation: Equal conditional distributions (0.60 passed in each class) show no association between class and passing.

diagram.caption: Results of an exam in two classes

stem: A table of the main way of getting news of 400 adults shows the row and column totals, but one entry is missing. What is the missing entry?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This is the number of adults under 40 who get news from television, in the same column.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This does not agree with the totals. The row must add to 200: 60 + 70 + 60 = 190.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is the column total for television, not the entry for one age group.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The row total for the adults who are 40 or over is 200, and 60 + 60 = 120 are the other entries, so the missing entry is 200 - 120 = 80. The column total, 130, gives 130 - 50 = 80 as well.

diagram.caption: Main way of getting news, for 400 adults

stem: In a two-way table of 400 adults, 120 are under 40 and get their news mainly online, 200 are under 40, and 180 get their news mainly online. Which of the following expressions is a conditional relative frequency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 200 / 400, the proportion of all of the adults who are under 40
choices.explanation: This is a row total divided by the table total, a marginal relative frequency.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 120 / 180, the proportion of the adults who get news online who are under 40
choices.explanation: A conditional relative frequency divides a cell by the total for the row or the column of interest.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 120 / 400, the proportion of all of the adults who are under 40 and get news online
choices.explanation: This divides by the table total, so it is a joint relative frequency.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 180 / 400, the proportion of all of the adults who get news online
choices.explanation: This is a column total divided by the table total, a marginal relative frequency.

explanation: Conditional: restrict to a level (the 180 who get news online) and divide by that total: 120 / 180.

stem: The table shows whether the members of a gym renewed their membership, by type of plan. Which of the following statements is supported by the summary statistics?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The members of the premium plan were more likely to renew than the members of the basic plan, because the premium plan has more members in it, and 90 is greater than 60
choices.explanation: The number of members in a plan does not decide the proportion who renewed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The members of the basic plan were more likely to renew, because 2/3 of the basic plan members renewed and 1/3 of the premium plan members renewed
choices.explanation: The conditional relative frequencies of renewing are 40 / 60 and 30 / 90, about 0.67 and 0.33.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The members of the basic plan were less likely to renew than the members of the premium plan, because 40 members renewed and 60 members did not renew, and 60 is greater than 40
choices.explanation: The 60 is the number of members in the basic plan, 40 + 20, and not the number who did not renew.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The two plans had the same proportion of the members who renewed, because 40 and 30 are close in the table
choices.explanation: The proportions are 0.67 and 0.33, which are not the same.

explanation: Compare the conditional relative frequencies of renewing: 40 / 60 for basic and 30 / 90 for premium.

diagram.caption: Membership renewals at a gym

stem: In a survey, 0.15 of all of the 400 adults are 40 or over and get their news mainly from print. A student says, "This means that 15% of the adults who are 40 or over get their news mainly from print." What is the error in the statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The 0.15 is a joint relative frequency, based on all 400 adults. The proportion of the adults who are 40 or over who get news from print is 60 / 200 = 0.30, a conditional relative frequency
choices.explanation: To describe a group, divide by the total for that group. The group of adults who are 40 or over has 200 adults.

choices.label: B
choices.text: There is no error, because a relative frequency always describes the group that it is about, whatever the total used
choices.explanation: The total used to divide matters: a joint relative frequency describes all of the individuals in the table.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The 0.15 should be a percent of the adults under 40, because print is a way of getting news that is chosen only by younger adults
choices.explanation: Nothing in the statement or the table limits print to younger adults.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The 0.15 is a marginal relative frequency, so it describes the adults who get news from print, whatever their age
choices.explanation: A marginal relative frequency divides a row total or a column total by the table total. The 0.15 uses a single cell.

explanation: A joint relative frequency is out of the whole table; the proportion within the 40-or-over group is 60 / 200 = 0.30.

stem: A spinner is spun 1,000 times and lands on red 312 times. Which of the following is the best estimate of the probability that the spinner lands on red on a single spin?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A probability of 0.50 would be right only if red and not red were equally likely, and nothing says that.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is the number of times that the spinner landed on red, not a probability.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is the relative frequency of the spins that did not land on red.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The probability of an outcome is estimated by its relative frequency over a large number of trials: 312 / 1,000.

explanation: Estimated probability = 312 / 1,000 = 0.312.

stem: Which of the following statements best describes the law of large numbers?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In any set of independent trials, the number of times that an outcome occurs is equal to the probability times the number of trials
choices.explanation: The count only tends to be close to this value, and it need not be equal to it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In a small number of trials the relative frequency of an outcome is always equal to the probability of the outcome
choices.explanation: A relative frequency from a small number of trials can be far from the probability.

choices.label: C
choices.text: After a long run of one outcome, the other outcomes become more likely, so the results balance out over the next few trials
choices.explanation: Independent trials do not remember earlier results, so the next trial is not affected.

choices.label: D
choices.text: For independent trials, as the number of trials increases, the relative frequency of an outcome gets closer and closer to a single value
choices.explanation: The single value is the probability of the outcome.

explanation: The law of large numbers is about relative frequencies of independent trials getting closer to a single value.

stem: A basketball player makes 70% of free throws. A student plans to use a random digit table, in which each of the digits 0 to 9 is equally likely, to simulate one free throw by this player. Which of the following assignments is appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Let the digits 0 through 2 represent a made free throw and the digits 3 through 9 represent a missed free throw
choices.explanation: Three of the ten digits have probability 0.30, which would be the probability of a miss.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Let the digits 0 through 7 represent a made free throw and the digits 8 and 9 represent a missed free throw
choices.explanation: Eight of the ten digits have probability 0.80, not 0.70.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Let the digits 0 through 6 represent a made free throw and the digits 7 through 9 represent a missed free throw
choices.explanation: Seven of the ten digits have probability 0.70, and three of the ten have probability 0.30.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Let the digits 0 through 4 represent a made free throw and the digits 5 through 9 represent a missed free throw
choices.explanation: Five of the ten digits have probability 0.50, so a made free throw would be as likely as a miss.

explanation: The digits assigned to a made free throw must have probability 0.70: seven of the ten digits.

stem: To estimate the probability that a family with 3 children has exactly 2 girls, a student lets each odd digit in a random digit table represent a girl and each even digit represent a boy. Which of the following describes one trial of the simulation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Read 3 digits and count how many of them are odd. Record whether the count is exactly 2
choices.explanation: A trial simulates one family: three children, each with a probability of 0.5 of being a girl.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Read 3 digits and add them. Record whether the sum is exactly 2
choices.explanation: The sum of the digits does not count the children who are girls.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Read 2 digits and record whether both of them are odd, as an estimate for 2 girls in a family of 3
choices.explanation: A family has 3 children, so 3 digits should be read in a trial.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Read 1 digit and record whether it is odd, and repeat this until the student has found exactly 2 odd digits in a row
choices.explanation: A trial must model one family with 3 children, not a run of digits.

explanation: Each trial reads three digits (one for each child), counts the odd ones, and records whether the count is 2.

stem: A player makes 70% of free throws. The dotplot shows the number of free throws made out of 10 attempts in each of 40 simulated trials. Based on the simulation, what is the estimated probability that the player makes at least 8 of 10 free throws?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: 17 of the 40 trials had 8 or more made free throws: 17 / 40.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is the relative frequency of the trials with fewer than 8 made free throws: 23 / 40.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This counts only the trials with exactly 8 made free throws: 8 / 40.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is the number of trials with at least 8 made free throws, not a probability.

explanation: Estimated probability = 17 / 40 = 0.425.

diagram.altText: Dotplot of the number of free throws made out of 10, in each of 40 simulated trials.

stem: The probability that a certain bus arrives late is 0.20. Which of the following is a correct interpretation of this probability?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The bus arrives on time on 20% of the days, because 0.20 is the probability that the bus arrives at the stop
choices.explanation: The 0.20 is the probability that the bus is late.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Over a very large number of days, the bus arrives late on about 20% of the days
choices.explanation: A probability is the long-run relative frequency of an outcome.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The bus arrives late on 20 days out of every 100 days, with the same number of late days in every set of 100 days
choices.explanation: The number of late days varies from one set of days to another. Only the long-run proportion is about 20%.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The bus arrives late on exactly 1 day out of every 5 days, so after 4 days on time the next day it will be late
choices.explanation: Probability describes the long run. It does not guarantee a pattern in a short run.

explanation: A probability of 0.20 means that, in the long run, about 20% of the days the bus arrives late.

stem: Which of the following is an event, but is not a single outcome, when a fair six-sided die is rolled once?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rolling a 6
choices.explanation: This is a single outcome, the result of one trial.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rolling the die one time
choices.explanation: This is the random process, not a result of it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rolling a 3
choices.explanation: This is a single outcome, the result of one trial.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rolling an odd number
choices.explanation: An event is a collection of outcomes. Rolling an odd number is made up of the outcomes 1, 3 and 5.

explanation: An event is a collection of outcomes; rolling an odd number is {1, 3, 5}.

stem: The table shows the number of boys in each of 200 simulated families with 4 children. Based on the simulation, what is the estimated probability that a family with 4 children has at least 3 boys?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The trials with 3 or 4 boys number 50 + 16 = 66, and 66 / 200 = 0.33.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This counts only the families with exactly 3 boys: 50 / 200.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is the relative frequency of the families with at most 2 boys: 134 / 200.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This counts only the families with 4 boys: 16 / 200.

explanation: Estimated probability = (50 + 16) / 200 = 0.33.

diagram.caption: Results of 200 simulated families with 4 children

stem: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled, one red and one green, and the number on each die is recorded. How many outcomes are in the sample space?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This is 6 + 6. The outcomes are pairs of numbers, so the counts are multiplied.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This counts the pairs without regard to which die has which number, but the red and the green die are different.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Each of the 6 outcomes of the red die can be paired with each of the 6 outcomes of the green die: 6 x 6 = 36.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is the number of possible sums, 2 through 12, not the number of outcomes.

explanation: The sample space has 6 x 6 = 36 equally likely outcomes.

stem: A bag has 5 red marbles, 3 blue marbles and 2 green marbles. One marble is selected at random. What is the probability that the marble is blue?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This is the probability that the marble is not blue: 7 / 10.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is 3 / 5, which compares the blue marbles with only the red marbles.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The outcomes are equally likely, so the probability is the number of favorable outcomes divided by the total: 3 / 10.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is 3 / 7, which compares the blue marbles with the 7 marbles that are not blue instead of with all 10 marbles.

stem: The probability that it rains on a given day in a city is 0.35. What is the probability that it does not rain on that day?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The probability of the complement of an event is 1 minus the probability of the event: 1 - 0.35.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This adds 1 and 0.35. A probability cannot be greater than 1.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is 0.35 / 0.65, a ratio of the two probabilities instead of the probability.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is the probability that it rains, the event itself.

stem: Which of the following could NOT be the probability of an event?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A probability of 0 is possible: it is the probability of an event that cannot happen.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is between 0 and 1, so it can be a probability.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A probability of 1 is possible: it is the probability of an event that is certain.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A probability is a number between 0 and 1, inclusive.

explanation: The probability of an event is a number between 0 and 1, inclusive, so 1.25 is not possible.

stem: A random process has four possible outcomes that do not overlap, with probabilities 0.20, 0.35, 0.10 and x. What is the value of x?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This is 1 - 0.55, which leaves out a probability. The three given probabilities add to 0.65.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is 1 divided by 4, which assumes that the four outcomes are equally likely. They are not.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is the sum of the other three probabilities, 0.20 + 0.35 + 0.10, and not what remains.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The probabilities of all of the outcomes in the sample space add to 1: 1 - (0.20 + 0.35 + 0.10) = 0.35.

explanation: The probability of the sample space is 1: x = 1 - 0.65 = 0.35.

stem: A fair coin is flipped 3 times. What is the probability of getting at least one head?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This is the probability of a head on any single flip, not on three flips.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is the probability of 3 tails, the complement of the event.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is the probability of exactly 1 head, which is only one of the ways to get at least one.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Use the complement: the only way to get no heads is 3 tails, with probability (1/2)(1/2)(1/2) = 1/8, so P(at least one head) = 1 - 1/8 = 7/8.

explanation: P(at least one head) = 1 - P(no heads) = 1 - 1/8 = 0.875.

stem: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum of the two numbers is 7?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Six of the 36 equally likely outcomes have a sum of 7: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1). 6 / 36 is about 0.167.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is 3 / 36. It counts the pairs without regard to the order, but the outcomes (1,6) and (6,1) are different.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is 7 / 36, which uses the sum 7 as the number of favorable outcomes.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is 1 / 11, which treats the 11 possible sums as equally likely. They are not.

explanation: P(sum of 7) = 6 / 36, about 0.167.

stem: A standard deck of 52 cards has 12 face cards (jacks, queens and kings). One card is selected at random. What is the probability that the card is not a face card?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This is 12 / 40, which compares the face cards with the cards that are not face cards.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This assumes that a card is a face card or not with equal probability, but the two are not equally likely.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The complement of a face card has 52 - 12 = 40 outcomes: 40 / 52, about 0.769.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is the probability that the card is a face card, 12 / 52.

explanation: P(not a face card) = 1 - 12 / 52 = 40 / 52, about 0.769.

stem: A six-sided die is not fair. The probability of rolling a 6 is 0.25, and each of the other five numbers is equally likely. What is the probability of rolling a 2?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This is the probability of rolling a 6, not a 2.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is 1 / 6, which assumes that all of the six numbers are equally likely. The die is not fair.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is 0.75 / 6, which shares the remaining probability among six numbers instead of five.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The probabilities add to 1, so the other five numbers share 1 - 0.25 = 0.75. Each has 0.75 / 5 = 0.15.

stem: A single card is selected at random from a standard deck of 52 cards. Which of the following pairs of events is mutually exclusive?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The card is a heart, and the card is a spade
choices.explanation: No card is both a heart and a spade, so the events cannot occur at the same time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The card is a heart, and the card is a king
choices.explanation: The king of hearts is both, so the events can occur together.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The card is a face card, and the card is red
choices.explanation: A red jack, queen or king is both a face card and red.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The card is an ace, and the card is a spade
choices.explanation: The ace of spades is both an ace and a spade.

explanation: Mutually exclusive events cannot occur at the same time: P(heart and spade) = 0.

stem: For events A and B, P(A) = 0.30, P(B) = 0.40 and P(A and B) = 0.12. Which of the following is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A and B are mutually exclusive, because 0.12 is the product of 0.30 and 0.40
choices.explanation: A product that equals the joint probability shows independence, not that the events are mutually exclusive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A and B are not mutually exclusive, because P(A and B) is not 0
choices.explanation: Events are mutually exclusive only if the joint probability is 0. Here it is 0.12.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A and B are mutually exclusive, because P(A and B) is less than both P(A) and P(B)
choices.explanation: A joint probability is always less than or equal to each probability, so this does not show that the events are exclusive.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A and B are mutually exclusive, because 0.30 + 0.40 is less than 1
choices.explanation: The sum of two probabilities being less than 1 does not show anything about the joint probability.

explanation: Since P(A and B) = 0.12 is not 0, the events can occur together.

stem: In a school, 40% of the students take Spanish, 25% take French, and no student takes both languages. Which of the following is the best justification that taking Spanish and taking French are mutually exclusive events?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The sum of the probabilities is less than 1: 0.40 + 0.25 = 0.65
choices.explanation: Mutually exclusive events can have any sum. What matters is the probability that both happen.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The probability of Spanish is greater than the probability of French: 0.40 is greater than 0.25
choices.explanation: Comparing the two probabilities does not tell whether both can occur.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The joint probability is 0: P(Spanish and French) = 0
choices.explanation: Events are mutually exclusive if the probability that both occur is 0.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The joint probability is the product of the probabilities: 0.40 x 0.25 = 0.10
choices.explanation: A product would be the joint probability of independent events, and here no student takes both.

explanation: P(Spanish and French) = 0, so the events cannot occur together.

stem: A fair six-sided die is rolled once. Let A be the event that the number is even and let B be the event that the number is greater than 4. Which of the following is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A and B are not mutually exclusive, because rolling a 6 is in both events and P(A and B) = 1/6
choices.explanation: The outcome 6 is even and greater than 4, so the events can occur at the same time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A and B are mutually exclusive, because the numbers 5 and 6 that are greater than 4 are not all even
choices.explanation: Events are exclusive only if no outcome is in both, and the number 6 is in both.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A and B are not mutually exclusive, because P(A and B) = 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6
choices.explanation: The joint probability is not the sum of the two probabilities. Only the outcome 6 is in both, so it is 1/6.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A and B are mutually exclusive, because P(A) = 1/2 and P(B) = 1/3 are not equal
choices.explanation: Unequal probabilities do not make events mutually exclusive.

explanation: A = {2, 4, 6}, B = {5, 6}. The outcome 6 is in both, so P(A and B) = 1/6, which is not 0.

stem: For two events A and B that are mutually exclusive, with P(A) > 0 and P(B) > 0, which of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A and B are not independent, because P(A and B) = 0 is not equal to P(A) x P(B)
choices.explanation: Independent events have P(A and B) = P(A) P(B), which is greater than 0 here.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A and B are independent, because the occurrence of one does not change anything about the other
choices.explanation: If A occurs, B cannot occur, so knowing A does change the probability of B.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A and B are independent only when P(A) + P(B) = 1, which is the case for complements
choices.explanation: Independence depends on the joint probability, not on whether the probabilities add to 1.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A and B are independent, because P(A and B) = 0 is less than both P(A) and P(B)
choices.explanation: Independence requires that the joint probability equal the product of the probabilities.

explanation: Mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities cannot be independent: knowing that A occurred makes P(B) become 0.

stem: In probability, what does P(A and B), the joint probability of events A and B, represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The probability that neither event A nor event B occurs
choices.explanation: That is the probability of the complement of the union.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The probability that event A occurs or event B occurs, or both
choices.explanation: That is the probability of the union.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The probability that event A occurs, given that event B has occurred
choices.explanation: That is a conditional probability.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The probability that both event A and event B occur
choices.explanation: The joint probability is the probability of the intersection of A and B.

explanation: P(A and B) is the probability of the intersection: both occur.

stem: The table shows the main way of getting news of 400 adults. One adult is selected at random. Which of the following pairs of events is mutually exclusive?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The adult is under 40, and the adult is 40 or over
choices.explanation: No adult is in both age groups.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The adult is 40 or over, and the adult gets news mainly from print
choices.explanation: There are 60 adults who are 40 or over and get news mainly from print.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The adult is under 40, and the adult gets news mainly online
choices.explanation: There are 120 adults who are under 40 and get news mainly online.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The adult is under 40, and the adult gets news mainly from television
choices.explanation: There are 50 adults who are under 40 and get news mainly from television.

explanation: The two age groups do not overlap, so P(under 40 and 40 or over) = 0.

stem: For events A and B, P(B) = 0.40 and P(A and B) = 0.10. What is P(A | B), the probability of A given that B has occurred?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is the joint probability, P(A and B), which has not been divided by P(B).

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is the product 0.10 x 0.40, instead of the quotient.

stem: The table shows the preferred lunch of 200 students. One student is selected at random. Given that the student prefers a packed lunch, what is the probability that the student is in Grade 10?

stem: For events A and B, P(A) = 0.60 and P(B | A) = 0.30. What is P(A and B)?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This adds the two numbers. The joint probability is found by multiplying.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is 0.30 / 0.60, which divides the conditional probability by P(A).

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: By the general multiplication rule, P(A and B) = P(A) P(B | A) = 0.60 x 0.30.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is the conditional probability P(B | A), not the joint probability.

stem: Two cards are dealt, one after the other and without replacement, from a standard deck of 52 cards that has 4 aces. What is the probability that both cards are aces?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: P(first ace) = 4/52, and P(second ace | first ace) = 3/51, so P(both) = (4/52)(3/51) = 12/2,652.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is (4/52)(4/52), which treats the second draw as having the same probability as the first. The deck has one fewer ace and one fewer card.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This uses 8 aces instead of 4 on the first card, which is more than the number of aces in the deck.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This adds the two probabilities. Both cards must be aces, so the probabilities are multiplied.

stem: A bag has 6 red marbles and 4 blue marbles. Two marbles are selected at random, one after the other and without replacement. Given that the first marble is blue, what is the probability that the second marble is blue?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This is 4 / 10, the probability of blue on the first draw. The second draw is from a bag with one fewer marble.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is 4 / 9, which removes a marble from the total but not from the number of blue marbles.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: After a blue marble is removed, the bag has 9 marbles and 3 of them are blue: 3 / 9.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is 3 / 10, which removes the blue marble from the number of blue marbles but not from the total.

explanation: P(second blue | first blue) = 3 / 9, about 0.333.

stem: Of the students at a school, 30% take the bus to school. A student who takes the bus is late with probability 0.10, and a student who does not take the bus is late with probability 0.05. What is the probability that a randomly selected student takes the bus and is late?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: P(bus and late) = P(bus) P(late | bus) = 0.30 x 0.10.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This adds 0.30 and 0.10. The joint probability is the product.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is the probability that a student is late, 0.30(0.10) + 0.70(0.05). It includes the students who do not take the bus.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is P(late | bus), the conditional probability, not the joint probability.

stem: The probability that a student passes an exam, given that the student studied, is 0.90. Which of the following is a correct interpretation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A student who studies is certain to pass the exam, because 0.90 is close to 1
choices.explanation: A probability of 0.90 is not certainty.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Of all of the students, 90% studied and passed the exam
choices.explanation: That would be a joint probability, the proportion of all students who both studied and passed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Among the students who passed, the probability that a randomly selected student studied is 0.90
choices.explanation: That would be P(studied | passed), the conditional probability in the other direction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Among the students who studied, the probability that a randomly selected student passes is 0.90
choices.explanation: A conditional probability restricts to the students who satisfy the condition, here those who studied.

explanation: P(pass | studied) describes the students who studied.

stem: The table shows the preferred lunch of 200 students. One student is selected at random. Given that the student is in Grade 9, what is the probability that the student prefers a packed lunch?

choices.label: C

stem: The table shows the results of a medical test for 1,000 people. One person is selected at random. Given that the person tests positive, what is the probability that the person has the condition?

choices.explanation: This is 90 / 1,000, the probability of having the condition and testing positive.

choices.label: D

stem: Which of the following is a correct statement of the general multiplication rule for events A and B?

choices.label: A
choices.text: P(A and B) = P(A | B) / P(B)
choices.explanation: The conditional probability P(A | B) is P(A and B) / P(B), so this expression is not the joint probability.

choices.label: B
choices.text: P(A and B) = P(A) + P(B | A)
choices.explanation: The probabilities are multiplied, not added.

choices.label: C
choices.text: P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B), always
choices.explanation: This holds only for independent events. The general rule uses the conditional probability.

choices.label: D
choices.text: P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B | A)
choices.explanation: The probability that both occur is the probability of A times the probability of B given that A has occurred.

explanation: General multiplication rule: P(A and B) = P(A) P(B | A).

stem: Events A and B are independent, with P(A) = 0.50 and P(B) = 0.30. What is P(A and B)?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) P(B) = 0.50 x 0.30.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is the sum of the two probabilities. The joint probability of independent events is the product.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This would be the joint probability of mutually exclusive events, not of independent events.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is P(A or B) = 0.50 + 0.30 - 0.15, the probability of the union.

stem: The table shows the preferred lunch of 200 students. One student is selected at random. Are the events "the student is in Grade 10" and "the student prefers a packed lunch" independent?

choices.explanation: The joint probability is 90 / 200 = 0.45, so the events are not mutually exclusive.

choices.explanation: Independence does not depend on whether the probabilities are greater than 0.50. It depends on the joint probability.

choices.explanation: Independent events have a joint probability equal to the product of the probabilities.

stem: Events A and B are independent. Which of the following must be true?

choices.explanation: This holds only when P(A and B) = 0. Independent events with positive probabilities have P(A and B) > 0.

stem: For events A and B, P(A) = 0.40, P(B) = 0.35 and P(A and B) = 0.15. What is P(A or B)?

stem: Events A and B are independent, with P(A) = 0.30 and P(B) = 0.50. What is P(A or B)?

stem: A single card is selected at random from a standard deck of 52 cards. The deck has 13 hearts, 12 face cards, and 3 cards that are both hearts and face cards. What is the probability that the card is a heart or a face card?

stem: A basketball player makes each free throw with probability 0.60, and the shots are independent. The player attempts two free throws. What is the probability that the player makes at least one of them?

choices.label: A

stem: A fair six-sided die is rolled twice. Let A be the event that the first roll is a 4, and let B be the event that the sum of the two rolls is 7. Which of the following is correct?

choices.label: A

choices.explanation: Given that the first roll is 4, the sum is 7 when the second roll is 3, which has probability 1/6.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A and B are not independent, because the sum depends on the number on the first roll
choices.explanation: The sum does depend on the first roll, but the probability that the sum is 7 stays the same, 1/6, whatever the first roll is.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A and B are not independent, because the first roll is part of the outcomes for which the sum is 7
choices.explanation: Being related in this way does not make events dependent. Check whether P(B | A) = P(B).

choices.label: D
choices.text: A and B are independent, because P(B | A) = 1/6 is equal to P(B) = 6/36
choices.explanation: If the first roll is 4, the sum is 7 only when the second roll is 3, with probability 1/6. The probability of a sum of 7 is 6/36 = 1/6 whatever the first roll is.

explanation: P(B | A) = 1/6 = P(B), so the events are independent.

stem: For events A and B, P(A) = 0.40, P(B) = 0.50 and P(A or B) = 0.90. Which of the following is correct?

choices.explanation: The union does not need to be 1. The joint probability is 0, so the events are mutually exclusive.

choices.explanation: Independence needs P(A and B) = P(A) P(B) = 0.20, which is not 0.

stem: The table shows the probability distribution of a discrete random variable X, with one probability missing. What is P(X = 2)?

stem: Which of the following tables is a valid probability distribution for a discrete random variable X with the possible values 1, 2, 3 and 4?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The probabilities add to 1.05, which is more than 1.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Each probability is between 0 and 1, and they add to 1.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This adds to 0.90, so the probabilities do not add to 1.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This adds to 1, but a probability cannot be negative.

explanation: A probability distribution has probabilities between 0 and 1 that add to 1.

stem: The table shows the probability distribution of a discrete random variable X. What is the cumulative probability P(X ≤ 2)?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is P(X ≤ 1), which leaves out the value 2.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is P(X = 2), only one of the values that are less than or equal to 2.

stem: The table shows the probability distribution of a discrete random variable X. What is P(X > 1)?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This is P(X ≤ 1) = 0.10 + 0.30, the probability of the complement.

choices.label: C

stem: Two fair coins are flipped. Let X be the number of heads. Which of the following is the probability distribution of X?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This assumes that 0, 1 and 2 heads are equally likely. One head can happen in two ways.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The outcomes TT, HT, TH and HH are equally likely, so one head has two ways out of four.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Two heads is possible, with probability 0.25.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Two heads is one of four equally likely outcomes, so its probability is 0.25, not 0.50.

explanation: The sample space {TT, HT, TH, HH} gives P(0) = 1/4, P(1) = 2/4, P(2) = 1/4.

stem: The bar graph shows the probability distribution of the number of pets, X, of a randomly selected family. What is the probability that a family has at least 3 pets?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This is the probability of exactly 3 pets, which leaves out the families with 4 pets.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: At least 3 pets means 3 or 4 pets: 0.25 + 0.10.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is the probability of 4 pets, the tallest value on the right, only one of the values.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is the probability of at most 2 pets, 0.05 + 0.20 + 0.40, the complement.

stem: A simulation of 200 trials is used to estimate the probability distribution of a random variable X, the number of heads in 3 flips of a coin that may not be fair. Based on the simulation, what is the estimated probability that X is 2?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This is the relative frequency of the trials with X = 1.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The relative frequency of the trials with X = 2 is 81 / 200.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is the number of trials with X = 2, not a probability.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This divides by 161, the number of trials with at most 2 heads, instead of by all 200 trials.

stem: The table shows the probability distribution of X, the number of goals that a team scores in a game. What is the mean (expected value) of X?

choices.label: A

stem: The table shows the probability distribution of X, the number of goals that a team scores in a game. The mean of X is 1.75. What is the standard deviation of X?

choices.label: B

choices.label: D
